item.title: Speech Analytics: Why a Speech Analytics Service Can Transcribe a Conversation Correctly but Evaluate It Incorrectly
item.description:
One of the most common mistakes when choosing a speech analytics system is to evaluate it by the quality of audio transcription. You upload a recording. You get text. A few terms are recognized incorrectly, but overall the conversation is readable. It seems that the main technical task is solved. In practice, the most interesting part begins after transcription. Let's say a client asks a manager: — Is there an integration option with our CRM? — Yes, such an option is provided. — And how long will it take? — Usually not long. From the point of view of recognition, there is almost nothing to discuss here. Even a simple ASR model can reconstruct such a dialogue quite accurately. Now let's ask the system to evaluate the quality of the consultation. Did the manager answer the question? Yes. Did they find out which CRM is used? No. Did they clarify the integration requirements? No. Did they give a specific deadline? No. The phrase 'usually not long' does not contain any useful assessment of deadlines for the client. Read more

item.title: Why a voice bot on LLM still needs a classifier like Jev
item.description:
An LLM voice bot sounds pleasant, but it regularly stumbles on real calls. It might find a free slot and fail to book a client, or interrupt someone who is just thinking mid-sentence. Some of these decisions can be offloaded from the LLM to a fast classifier model. The most discussed one now is Jev from TypeSafe, and it already has open-source alternatives. Below, I analyze how other teams use Jev-like models in voice bots and compare their cases with our experience at Voximplant. Read more

item.title: Programming without an IDE, or using Qwen and Qwen Coder for software development
item.description:
We will try to quickly write an NTFS alternate data streams scanner using a non-trivial stack and architecture. I did this primarily to test the capabilities of the Qwen family of models. A brief explanation for those who haven't worked in this area. NTFS (an abbreviation for New Technology File System) is the standard file system for the Windows NT family of operating systems. One of its little-known features is the presence of Alternate Data Streams (ADS), which are metadata associated with an NTFS file system object. Thus, several data streams can be attached to a file that will not be visible through standard OS tools. Read more

item.title: Vibe coding vs. old school: what should designers do in the age of AI?
item.description:
A beginner designer asked me recently: should I learn WordPress to build websites from scratch? At first, I avoided the topic, suggesting they look at something newer, like Tilda or Webflow. I compared it to the situation in 2014, when there were few alternatives for building a website without coding knowledge. But then I decided. And I said what I was afraid to admit to myself: 'There is a serious possibility that our profession will soon cease to exist.' Why do courses still promise an easy entry into the industry, remote work from anywhere, and why do big tech leads earn money on consultations — and people go to them? Because, in my observation, the industry has split into two camps. They live in parallel universes, in one of which newcomers seek advice from seniors, confident in their indispensability. In the second — those who, without knowing the basics of web design, go and vibe-code websites, shining with the Dunning-Kruger effect, for which they get reprimanded by the 'old-timers.' By buying a ticket to the first, the newcomer is forced to move to the second, because employers increasingly demand proficiency in neural networks. And at the same time, senior designers scold in the comments works created through AI: 'It's impossible to generate a website that solves business problems without experience.' Quite recently, I also thought that with my vast experience, there was nothing to fear. Yeah) Read more

item.title: Can We Abandon Opus and Codex? I Tested MacBook, Gaming Laptop, and DGX Spark on One Tricky Task
item.description:
In my open-daimon pet project, routing between local and cloud models has long been available. I'll admit upfront: open-daimon isn't publicly updated because I develop it locally for speed. Based on it, I have a separate private project that expands its capabilities – an agent management studio. I tested everything there. The desire to do this seriously arose for a simple reason: the rules in the cloud are set by others and change without notice. In October, it resurfaced that Anthropic's consumer terms for EEA and Swiss residents explicitly state: do not use services 'for commercial or business purposes.' This applies to Claude.ai, Pro, and Max subscriptions. Thus, a developer in Europe writing working code in Claude Code with a Max subscription is formally violating them. For work, you need an API, Team, or Enterprise plan, which is a different league of cost. The second story is about what you're allowed to do with your own hardware. A Decrypt author asked Claude Opus 5.5 to help regain root access on their LG TV. The model's safety filters cut off the request and suggested switching to Opus 4.8. And a researcher, known for discovering a constantly active microphone in Samsung TVs, writes that OpenAI blocked his account for 'Cyber Abuse' after analyzing firmware via ChatGPT. Along with the account, about $500 in API balance disappeared. OpenAI hasn't commented, so for now, these are just his words. The direction is clear: probing third-party software will be increasingly forbidden, and the manufacturer decides what constitutes abuse. Read more

item.title: One Picture is a Masterpiece, a Hundred Pictures are a Catastrophe: How I Tried to Tame AI Asset Generation for an Indie RPG
item.description:
Developing an indie game is a constant struggle with resources. Usually, there isn't enough time, money, people, and, ideally, a couple more hours in the day. When I started making Morveyn (https://habr.com/ru/articles/1100432/) - a turn-based RPG for Telegram, inspired by classic fantasy strategies like King's Bounty - it quickly became clear that writing a game and filling it with content are two completely different tasks. The technical part was relatively clear: Next.js on the frontend, Java on the backend, game logic, server interaction, map generation. This is familiar territory for a developer. But the graphics turned out to be a separate adventure. The game needs dozens, and potentially hundreds, of images: units, character portraits, buildings, environmental objects, global map tiles, icons, and interface elements. Moreover, all of this must look as if it was created by a single artist for a single game. Hiring an artist for every experimental asset at the MVP stage was irrational. So I decided to try generative AI. Ultimately, Gemini became the main tool. And that's when the most interesting part began. Read more

item.title: LLM Conversations: Risk Propensity of Different Noo-spheres / LLMs
item.description:
Several works in the literature have studied the attitude of different noo-spheres / LLMs towards risk. This article presents a review of these works from the perspective of the author's developing LLM theory. Interestingly, although in the general case the task (prompt) influences the riskiness of the noo-sphere's behavior, for popular models with identical starting conditions, a pattern in the riskiness of their behavior has been found: Claude Sonnet 4.5 < DeepSeek V3.2 < Gemini 3 Pro < Qwen3 Max < GPT-5.2. item.title: From Prompt to Production in Two Hours: Everything You Need to Know About Claude Code
item.description:
By the end of 2026, Claude Code is no longer an exotic tool: Anthropic's CLI agent generates everything from videos and websites to applications, scripts, and articles, handling a significant portion of engineering routine. Some call it the best thing to happen to development in years; others point to limits that are reached faster than expected, complain about decisions the agent makes without permission, and the ongoing wave of account bans. This article is for those who haven't dived headfirst into the AI sphere and still copy code from browser to IDE, but now want to understand what Claude Code is all about. In this article, I'll explain how to use it, why a couple of hours instead of a couple of days is a realistic scenario for a small feature or service (I'll clarify this upfront). We'll cover what to configure before the first run, how to describe a project so the agent doesn't guess commands, and when it's time to stop and check everything manually. We'll also explore specific tools and innovations in Claude Code. Read more
